evidence.label: Cyclic length and chromatic fixed-point loss

headline: Claims the exact chromatic loss between fixed points of p-group actions is a count of cyclic steps.
scope: Every prime, every finite p-group G, every subgroup H and every height n at least 0, for finite genuine G-spectra.
plain: Smith theory says a group of prime-power order acting on a space carries certain properties over to its fixed points. Chromatic versions ask how many heights of information are lost on the way. The answer was known for abelian groups and some special cases. This paper claims the exact answer for every finite p-group: the shortest chain of cyclic steps from the subgroup H up to G. It confirms an equality proposed by Kuhn and Lloyd.
doesNot: This does not directly treat groups whose order is not a prime power; those need earlier reductions by Balmer and Sanders.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Edwin Floyd, periodic maps and Euler characteristics, a quantitative form of Smith theory
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles the equality Kuhn and Lloyd proposed for all finite p-groups, which pins down a key part of the equivariant Balmer spectrum.

explanation:
Take p = 2 and the group G = C₄ × C₂, with 8 elements. Here Cₖ is the cyclic group of k elements, the turns of a k-sided wheel. G has two different subgroups of order 2. One is H₁, generated by twice the generator of C₄. The other is H₂, the C₂ factor. Divide out by each one. G/H₁ is C₂ × C₂, which needs two cyclic steps to build. G/H₂ is C₄, which needs one step. The answer in this paper depends on exactly this count, 2 for H₁ and 1 for H₂.

Why count steps? Smith theory says that when a group of prime-power order acts on a finite space, mod-p acyclicity passes to the fixed points[10]. Acyclic here means having no holes as seen by mod-p homology. The chromatic version uses Morava K-theories K(n), one for each height n. These see finer and finer layers of stable homotopy. The loss is how many heights higher you must check the fixed points of H to force acyclicity of the fixed points of G. A chain of cyclic steps gives an upper bound, one height per step[7].

For abelian groups the answer was known. The loss equals the fewest generators of G/H[5]. For other groups a simple lower bound can be too small. In the eight-element symmetry group of a square, a subgroup of order 2 that is not central has loss two. The simple lower bound there is one[6]. The obstacle was proving that the chain bound is sharp for every embedded subgroup[8]. The usual character theory sees only abelian images, so it cannot reach this directly[9].

The paper claims that the optimal loss equals the shortest chain of cyclic steps from H to G[1]. This holds at every prime and every height. So the loss does not depend on the height[3]. It includes the rational case at height zero[11]. A cyclic step of order p² still counts once[4]. This confirms the equality Kuhn and Lloyd proposed[2].

How sure is this? There is no Lean check. A computer proof checker has not looked at any part of it. The proof combines delicate character theory with arithmetic constraints on profinite groups. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proof holds. It completes a known equality for all finite p-groups. There is no Lean check and no published specialist review.

glossary.meaning: A finite group whose number of elements is a power of the prime p.
The points of a space that a group of symmetries leaves in place.
Classical results that carry homology properties of a space over to its fixed points.
A homology theory that sees one chromatic height n of stable homotopy.
Having no holes as seen by a given homology theory.
A chain of subgroups where each is normal in the next one.
How many heights must be added at the subgroup to force acyclicity at the whole group.
